places.name: 1921 Mount Dora
places.address: 1921 Mount Dora, 142 E 4th Ave, Mt Dora, FL 32757-5584
places.description: Dinner here feels like being welcomed into an elegant friend's home, which is exactly what this century-old house wants you to feel. 1921 Mount Dora pairs the charm of a historic 1921 home with modern Florida cuisine built on local farms, and the kitchen cooks like it has something to prove. Order the Spanish octopus with hazelnut romesco, the wood-oven roasted oysters with BLT butter, and the Wagyu burger with smoked Duke's mayonnaise. Every bite tastes like Florida telling its own story, and it is a story worth savoring.

places.name: 600 Block
places.address: Universal CityWalk (inside Pat O'Brien's)
places.description: Most people walk straight past it inside Pat O'Brien's, and that is the point. 600 Block is CityWalk's password-door speakeasy, 21 and up, tucked behind the dueling-piano noise into something smokier and slower, where a jazz musician sets the tempo and the cocktails get the same care as the secrecy. Sit outside if you want the piano drifting up from downstairs and CityWalk people-watching at its finest, sit inside if you want the full hushed, dimly lit spell. It keeps vanishing and returning, so when the door is open, you go.

places.name: Amar Orlando
places.address: 8001 S Orange Blossom Trl, Ste #1510, Orlando, FL 32809
places.description: Amar is the kind of Mediterranean kitchen where everything tastes like it came straight off the fire and out of somebody's family recipe box. Olive oil that actually tastes like olives, shawarma shaved with intent, pita still warm enough to steam when you tear it, and salads that crunch instead of wilt. The room runs on that bright, generous Levantine hospitality where you are fed like a guest, not a transaction. When you want a bowl of food that leaves you feeling better than it found you, this is the stop.

places.name: Amare
places.address: Amare, 1255 Epcot Resorts Blvd, Orlando, FL 32830
places.description: Walk into Amare and the Disney bubble dissolves into something calmer and older: olive trees in your mind, sea air in your glass. Chef Scott West's kitchen treats the Mediterranean as a journey, not a theme, plates that swing from grilled coastal fish to slow, earthy braises, each one with a pour to match from a wine list built entirely around the region. Ask about the curated flights, they are the shortcut to tasting Greece, Italy and Spain in a single sitting. It is the rare resort restaurant that earns the trip on its own.

places.name: American Social
places.address: Doctor Phillips
places.description: American Social is where Restaurant Row lets its hair down. Equal parts sports bar, restaurant and live-music stage, it runs on high voltage: big screens in every sightline, a bar pouring hand-crafted cocktails and local beer, and a kitchen that treats bar food like it matters, burgers with actual char, croquetas worth ordering twice. Regulars mix with first-timers from the theme parks, and the room is built for that exact collision, conversations you didn't plan and nights that run later than intended.

places.name: Aphrodisiaco
places.address: International Drive, Orlando, FL 32819
places.description: Aphrodisiaco takes its name from the goddess of love and plays the part completely. This is an I-Drive speakeasy built for romance done properly: warm low light, music that pulls you closer instead of drowning you out, and a kitchen that thinks in elements, fire, sea, earth, with handcrafted cocktails built to match the mood of the plate. It is the reservation you make when the night matters and you want every sense leaned into the evening. Dress well, the room expects it of you.

places.name: Bacán
places.address: Bacán, Higgs Aly, Orlando, FL 32827
places.description: Say the name and watch Lake Nona sit up straighter. BACÁN is an immersive affair built around a dramatic open theater kitchen, where Chef Guillaume Robin, honored as a Maître Cuisinier de France, and Sous Chef Ryne Wood turn the boldly seductive flavors of the Americas into edible theater. Order the whole Florida snapper, save room for the banana tart finished with gold leaf, and watch a chocolate sphere melt open at your table. Elevated yet approachable, innovative and just a little bit unexpected, this is a night out that alters your perception.

places.name: Banh Mi Boy
places.address: 1110 E Colonial Dr, Orlando, FL 32803
places.description: Michelin handed it a Bib Gourmand, Netflix's Somebody Feed Phil came with cameras, but Banh Mi Boy never changed its tune. This Mills Market fixture, serving for over twenty years, bakes baguettes that shatter and sigh the way Saigon street bread should, then loads them with crispy pork belly, roasted garlic mayo and house pate. The playful side shows in the pho French dip, a whole sandwich begging to be dunked in rich broth, and fresh-pressed sugarcane juice that tastes like afternoon in Vietnam. This is Orlando's Vietnamese soul, perfected over decades.

places.name: Banh Mi Cali
places.address: Banh Mi Cali, 5210 W Colonial Dr, Orlando, FL 32808-7606
places.description: No frills, no pretense, just one of Orlando's most honest banh mi counters. The sandwiches come on crisp, airy baguettes stuffed with the classics, roast pork, meatballs, house pate and terrine, with pickled carrot and daikon crunching through every bite. Regulars round it out with a strong Vietnamese iced coffee or a milk tea, and the doughnuts earn their own quiet reputation. It is small, fast, and exactly the kind of unassuming lunch spot locals protect like a secret.

places.name: Beefy King
places.address: Beefy King, 424 N Bumby Ave, Orlando, FL 32803-6028
places.description: Every city has a sandwich shop its people would defend in a fistfight, and in Orlando that shop is Beefy King. Since 1968, Freeman and Margaret Smith's counter on Bumby Avenue has been steaming roast beef until it falls apart in a good way, piling it onto soft, steamed kaiser rolls with diced onions, and sending it out with Beefy Spuds, crisp tater tots by another name, and chili that tastes like decades of practice. It survived an arson fire and came back swinging. Go for lunch and understand why nobody here touches the drive-thru chain version.

places.name: Black Bean Deli
places.address: 1835 E Colonial Dr, Orlando, FL 32803
places.description: Owner Andres Corton built this place from his grandparents' kitchen and the spirit of those 1960s Miami cafes with their ventanitas, and you taste that lineage in everything. The pan con lechon arrives stacked with mojo-kissed pulled pork, the empanadas crackle with seasoned picadillo, and the guava pastelito is flaky without cloying. Order a cafe con leche and do it the Cuban way, strong, sweet, made for sharing. This is the Cuban cooking Orlando's Cuban families hold up as the real thing.

places.name: Blue Man Group
places.address: ICON Park, 8375 International Dr, Orlando, FL 32819
places.description: Paint drums splatter in rhythm, tubes thump overhead, and without a word three blue performers pull the audience into the joke. Blue Man Group plays in its new custom theater at ICON Park on I-Drive, a wordless mix of drums, paint, and participation for all ages. It fits most groups — bring kids or grandparents, sit back from the splash zone, and stay out at ICON Park after. Tourist Trail: Worth it — a fresh room for a show that still works.

places.name: Bombay Street Kitchen
places.address: 6215 S Orange Blossom Trl, Orlando
places.description: Forget the tired curry-house playbook. Bombay Street Kitchen, from chef Amit Kumar of the beloved Aashirwad and Tamarind, is a love letter to the street carts of Mumbai, Delhi, Chennai and Bangalore, and Michelin noticed, awarding it a Bib Gourmand. The menu reads like a food tour: Dahi Bhalla Papri Chaat with its tangle of tangy, crunchy, cool; crispy Kurkuri Bhindi Bhel with pomegranate popping through; tandoori momos with real char. Save room for the falooda, rose syrup, vermicelli and rabdi in a glass. This is India beyond the clichés, on Orange Blossom Trail.

places.name: Boxi Park Lake Nona
places.address: 6877 Tavistock Lakes Blvd, Orlando, FL 32827
places.description: Someone looked at forty-foot shipping containers and saw Lake Nona's best party, and they were right. Boxi Park stacks the boxes into a one-of-a-kind open-air hangout where you can graze lobster rolls from Claw & Order, tacos from Canonita, and housemade burgers while a live band plays and the dog races around the pup park. The lineup never sits still, with rotating pop-ups under the Before It's Gone banner, beach volleyball, and drinks from Bar Nona and Hops and Vine. Bring everyone.

places.name: Briarpatch
places.address: Briarpatch Restaurant, 252 N Park Ave, Winter Park, FL 32789-3814
places.description: Since 1980, Briarpatch has been the Park Avenue breakfast institution, and owner John Pertz runs it like the French Culinary Institute graduate he is: brioche baked in-house with honey and lemon zest, premium olive oil and clarified butter instead of shortcuts, avocados chosen with obsessive care. The famous French toast comes stuffed with raspberry and brie, the pancakes wear raspberry lemon cream, and the short rib Benedict has ruined lesser Benedicts for generations of Rollins students. The covered patio is Winter Park at its most civilized. Take home a slice of peanut butter pie, trust us.

places.name: Buttermilk Bakery
places.address: Buttermilk Bakery, 1198 Orange Ave, Winter Park, FL 32789-4908
places.description: The ovens fire up at 4 AM, and every layer shows it. Buttermilk Bakery is the Rebroff family's love letter to European baking, run by Brazilian matriarch Lana with her children Phillip, Taissa and Alex, and the small-batch croissants shatter like they should, rivals of anything from Paris. The case rotates with the seasons, pumpkin cheesecake croissants in fall, strawberry rhubarb tarts in spring, plus fluffy brioche donuts and savory khachapuri for the non-sweet crowd. Get there before the devotees do, because the best trays sell out and nobody is coming back tomorrow for leftovers.

places.name: Camille
places.address: Camille, 4962 New Broad St, Orlando, FL 32814-6415
places.description: Chef Tung Phan named his restaurant for his eldest daughter and cooks like he is honoring the name. Camille earned a Michelin star for its singular vision: the vibrant food culture of Vietnam presented in a refined, progressive form, with French technique woven through every course. The eight-seat chef's counter is theater, pho reimagined with wagyu tartare and savory broth, red bean desserts that play like a cheese course. It started as a pop-up before it had a restaurant, and the daring never left. For a milestone night, few Orlando rooms feel this considered.

places.name: Capa
places.address: Four Seasons
places.description: Seventeen floors up inside the Four Seasons, Capa makes a case that the great steakhouse tradition belongs to Spain too. Chefs Fabrizio Schenardi and Chris Edwards cook over a wood-burning grill in an open kitchen, sending out Wagyu from Florida's own Clear Creek Farm alongside tapas that show off: fried cauliflower with capers and a fried egg, pork cheeks with Marcona almonds. Start with cocktails on the rooftop terrace, where the view stretches over golf greens and wetlands to the nightly Disney fireworks. Dark wood, black and crimson, candlelight, the whole romantic apparatus, earned.

places.name: Casa Mezcal
places.address: International Drive, Orlando, FL 32819
places.description: Casa Mezcal plays the name straight: the spirit is the headliner and the kitchen backs it up. On I-Drive's busiest stretch, this is the late-night Mexican room with a full bar pouring mezcal and tequila with conviction, tacos built for proper pairings, and a scene that leans festive once the sun goes down. The room hums with music and conversation, the kind of place where dinner slides into drinks without anyone deciding to stay. Dress up a little, come hungry, and let the night run.

places.name: Cañonita
places.address: 6877 Tavistock Lakes Blvd, Orlando, FL 32827
places.description: Cañonita comes with a pedigree: the brand was born at The Venetian in Las Vegas, where it paired canal-front dining with Mexico City street food and one of the Strip's deep tequila lists. In Lake Nona it wears two faces, the walk-up Cañonita Street Taqueria inside Boxi Park, all street tacos, nachos and chips with salsa under the string lights, and a full-service Cañonita at Lake Nona West run by the Tavistock Restaurant Collection. Grab a few tacos, a margarita from the Boxi Park bar, and let the whole crew order something different.

places.name: Celine Orlando
places.address: Downtown
places.description: Celine is downtown's answer to the question of where the night goes when it wants options. Three levels on Magnolia Avenue: a Prohibition-era speakeasy tucked below, a grand ballroom with chandeliers and full-throttle light design, and the crown jewel, a rooftop lounge where DJs play to open sky and the downtown towers. Craft cocktails flow across all three, and the crowd is a downtown mix, concerts one night, DJ sets the next, celebrations always. Pick your floor, or wander between them all.

places.name: Charles Hosmer Morse Museum of American Art
places.address: 445 N Park Ave, Winter Park, FL 32789
places.description: Modest from the street, breathtaking inside: the Morse holds the world's most comprehensive collection of Louis Comfort Tiffany, and standing in its galleries you understand why people make pilgrimages. Hugh and Jeannette McKean salvaged truckloads of art and architecture from Tiffany's fire-ravaged Long Island estate and brought it here, including the Byzantine-Romanesque chapel interior built for Chicago's 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. Lamps, leaded-glass windows, iridescent vases that shift color as you move. It is the soul of Winter Park's arts claim, and it quietly earns the title.

places.name: Chathams Place
places.address: Chatham's Place, 7575 Dr Phillips Blvd, Orlando, FL 32819-5149
places.description: Old-school fine dining survives in this Dr. Phillips dining room, and that is exactly the point. Chatham's Place is independently owned, chef-driven, and unapologetically classic: Chef Tony's kitchen sends out lobster salad, center-cut filet and off-menu treasures like pesto Parmesan pasta twirled tableside inside a whole wheel of cheese. A live pianist fills the dim, intimate room, and the service treats anniversaries like the sacred occasions they are. This is where Orlando's special nights have been going for nearly thirty years.

places.name: Chef Mickey's
places.address: Chef Mickey's, 4600 N World Dr, Orlando, FL 32830-8413
places.description: Some Disney memories are manufactured, but the joy in this room is real. Chef Mickey's sits on the Contemporary Resort's grand concourse, monorail gliding right through the building, and every meal is a celebration: Mickey, Minnie, Goofy, Pluto and Donald working the tables while the whole room twirls napkins overhead to music. The buffet does the heavy lifting, breakfast spreads and dinner carving stations built for refills and second plates. For a kid meeting Mickey Mouse up close, there is no substitute. Book early, the world knows about this one.

places.name: Coro
places.address: Coro, 3022 Corrine Dr, Orlando, FL 32803-2204
places.description: The name means chorus, and the menu sings in one. Chef Tim Lovero's Audubon Park gem earned a Michelin Bib Gourmand for small plates that change with the seasons and the chef's mood: warm potato naan with whipped chicken skin butter and marmalade, lamb shoulder so tender it surrenders, and a dessert that riffs on fries and a milkshake with panna cotta, crispy sunchoke and cocoa nibs. The open kitchen puts the cooks within arm's reach, and the wine list leans natural. Intimate, evolving, and exactly what a neighborhood restaurant should be.

places.name: Cowboy Curry
places.address: 1110 E Colonial Dr, Orlando, FL 32803
places.description: From the UniGirl family comes a love letter to Japanese curry done the slow way: forty hours, forty ingredients, and a sauce sweetened only with fruits and vegetables, no gluten, no dairy, just depth. The base curry is beef, slow-cooked to silk, and then you build: chicken katsu with real crunch, gyu katsu, fried karaage, fried oyster. The bowl arrives deep and steaming, and a cup of hojicha tea on the side is the move. Comfort food with an obsession behind it, in the middle of Mills Market's chaos.

places.name: Cups and Pups
places.address: 2413 Edgewater Dr, Orlando, FL 32804
places.description: From a roadside cart to an airstream to this bright Edgewater Drive shop, Cups and Pups has grown up without losing its charm. The menu runs on joy: a Honey Nut Cheerio Latte that tastes like the bottom of the cereal bowl, a Brown Sugar Pop Tart Latte, lavender cold brew, and rotating seasonal creations, all built on Lineage Coffee. The dog-friendly patio lets you order from your seat without leaving your pup's side, and inside, the dog-face logo cutout is pure photo bait. Laptop-friendly, tail-friendly, neighborhood through and through.

places.name: Domu
places.address: 3201 Corrine Dr, Orlando, FL 32803
places.description: Since November 2016, Domu has been the ramen room Orlando talks about. The East End Market original earned a Michelin Bib Gourmand and a Netflix spotlight, and the bowls live up to it. Start with the kimchi butter wings, then the Richie Rich ramen, and give yourself over to the broth. The room is compact, the line is real, and first come first serve keeps the energy honest. Worth every minute of the wait.

places.name: Dr. Phillips Center for the Performing Arts
places.address: 445 S Magnolia Ave, Orlando, FL 32801
places.description: For decades Orlando proved it could fill stadiums, but nobody knew if it could fill a concert hall night after night. Then Dr. Phillips Center opened in 2014 and answered that question for good. Broadway tours light up the Walt Disney Theater, Steinmetz Hall pours out symphony sound with pristine acoustics, and the Judson's Live cabaret room keeps the late nights intimate. This is the two block stretch where Orlando found its cultural heartbeat.

places.name: Edoboy
places.address: 728 N Thornton Ave, Orlando, FL 32803
places.description: Eight seats, no chairs, one hour, twelve pieces of some of the best sushi in Florida. Edoboy is Orlando's first standing sushi bar, chef Sean "Sonny" Nguyen's passion project inspired by his travels through Tokyo, Osaka and Kyoto, where standing sushi is the local's shortcut to excellence. You book a slot on Resy, stand at the counter, and order nigiri and hand rolls from the chefs piece by piece, each one brushed and ready. Finish with miso soup made from the fish bones of the day and, if you are wise, the matcha s'more. Fast, fun, and fiercely good.

places.name: El Cilantrillo
places.address: El Cilantrillo Restaurant, 1301 Florida Mall Ave, Orlando, FL 32809-7731
places.description: Orlando's Boricua community has a big table and it is here. El Cilantrillo is Puerto Rican comfort in full color: mofongo stuffed and towering, the massive chuleta kan kan, churrasco off the plancha, arroz con gandules that tastes like somebody's grandmother is still watching the pot. Live salsa music rolls through the dining room, the coconut mojitos are notorious, and their own Don Turull Café pours island coffee dedicated to the founder's father. If you want to taste Puerto Rico without boarding a plane, start here.

places.name: Enzo's On the Lake
places.address: Enzo's on the Lake, 1130 S US Highway 17 92, Longwood, FL 32750-5718
places.description: On the shore of Lake Kathryn in Longwood, Enzo's has been Central Florida's special-occasion Italian since 1980, and it has only gotten better at the job. The dining room glows warm, the La Terrazza deck sits right at the water for sunset, and the kitchen cooks with old-world confidence: bucatini alla Enzo, Dover sole that regulars swear is the finest they've had anywhere, a wine list deep enough to get lost in. Live music drifts across the lake after dinner. Some restaurants are meals; this one is an evening.

places.name: Eola Food Hall
places.address: Lake Eola, Orlando, FL (historic University Club building)
places.description: Downtown's newest food hall lives in the bones of the old University Club, the 1926 social club that watched a century of Orlando go by. Thirteen vendor stalls fill the lower floor, a speakeasy and wine bar perch on the second, and the whole thing was built to be a destination, with events, musicians and DJs in the mix. First in the door was Croissant Gourmet, bringing authentic French pastry, five kinds of French toast and nine varieties of crepes, to its first Orlando location. Steps from the Lake Eola skyline, this is downtown eating, upgraded.

places.name: EPCOT
places.address: 200 Epcot Center Dr, Orlando, FL 32830
places.description: Walt's grandest what-if, still standing. EPCOT opened in 1982 as the Experimental Prototype Community of Tomorrow, his World's Fair dream of a city of the future, and four neighborhoods carry that ambition now: celebration, discovery, nature, and the World Showcase, where eleven countries ring a lagoon in an afternoon walk around the planet. Come during a festival, Flower and Garden in spring, Food and Wine in fall, when the park becomes one long global tasting menu, and stay for the nighttime spectacular over the water. It is the most human of Disney's parks, curiosity made into a place.

places.name: Everoak Farm
places.address: Everoak Farm, 2335 Carrington Dr, Orlando, FL 32807
places.description: Ten minutes from downtown, three acres of soil are doing something radical. Husband-and-wife team Mike and Nikki Garcia run EverOak as a regenerative, biointensive family farm, no sprays, bees working the rows, pasture-raised chickens roaming, Certified Naturally Grown produce pulled from living soil. Their Saturday market is a genuine community gathering, fellow small businesses popping up alongside the farm stand, and their CSA feeds seventy local families while their harvest shows up on restaurant menus across town. If you want to taste where Orlando's farm-to-table actually starts, it starts here.

places.name: Fat One's Hot Dogs & Italian Ice
places.address: Universal CityWalk
places.description: Yes, that Joey Fatone. The *NSYNC member and Orlando native opened his first permanent restaurant at CityWalk on September 19, 2026, with his longtime manager Joe Mulvihill, and the hot dogs go far beyond ballpark fare. Nine loaded creations: The Fat One, a footlong buried under roasted pork, pepperoni, chili beans, cheddar cheese sauce and pop fries; The Brazilian, grilled linguica with Calabrian honey and jalapeño veganaise; the Dirty K-Pop Dog with kimchi slaw and gochujang mayo. Cool it down with old-school Italian ice and a specialty beer. Pure Orlando pop-culture joy.

places.name: Flatlands Bar & Grill
places.address: Flamingo Crossings Village
places.description: Brand new at Flamingo Crossings, and already worth leaving the Disney bubble for. From restaurateur Nick Valenti with executive chef Dominique Filoni, formerly of Disney's Cítricos and Topolino's Terrace, Flatlands is built around Central Florida's 1920s citrus boom: the building looks like a vintage packing facility, and the cooking follows the Italian-immigrant principles behind it, great ingredients, simple preparations, zero compromise. The Maine lobster rolls are the breakout star, the cookie skillet finishes strong, and the Orange Blossom Collins drinks like Florida itself. Disney-adjacent dining, all grown up.

places.name: Foreigner Restaurant
places.address: Foreigner Restaurant, 2816 Corrine Dr, Orlando, FL 32803-2226
places.description: Chef Bruno Fonseca's Brazilian roots run through this Corrine Drive counter like a current. Foreigner is a chef's-counter tasting room serving a menu confiance, a monthly-changing parade of globally inspired courses, where poached oysters meet caviar and brown butter powder, mackerel gets the moqueca treatment, and picanha lands with bordelaise and morels. It began as intimate popups, and the intimacy survived the move to a permanent room: Chef Bruno introduces each course personally, the wine pairings are chosen with real care, and you leave feeling like a houseguest who was fussed over beautifully.

places.name: Four Flamingos
places.address: Four Flamingos, 1 Grand Cypress Blvd, Orlando, FL 32836
places.description: Chef Richard Blais brought his first Florida kitchen to the Hyatt Regency Grand Cypress, and it is exactly as playful as you'd hope. The dining room feels like a dreamy tropical oasis, with an open kitchen, a raw bar, and a live lobster tank to stare into while you wait. The menu chases Florida's bounty: Tuna Tostada crowned with a passion fruit yolk, bone-in swordfish prime rib, coconut and mango running through everything. Order the Key Lime in the Coconut cocktail and stay for the laid-back, linger-long energy.

places.name: Francesco's Ristorante
places.address: Maitland
places.description: Palermo-born chef Francesco Aiello trained at Sicily's prestigious Istituto Alberghiero, opened his Maitland namesake in 2012, and just swept five awards, including Best Italian in Florida and Best Local Chef. The proof is in the open flame: wood-burning ovens blister hand-tossed Margheritas, pastas are rolled by hand, mozzarella is made in-house, and the kitchen turns out gnocchi Siciliana, spaghetti alle vongole, and a tableside Pinwheel Reggiano Flambéed Pappardella that is pure theater. Chef Francesco plates in the open kitchen and works the room like family. This is Maitland's pride, and it eats like it.

places.name: Fluffy Fluffy Dessert Cafe
places.address: 2008 E Colonial Dr, Orlando, FL
places.description: Fuwa fuwa means fluffy fluffy in Japanese, and the name is a promise kept. This dessert cafe, founded by Benson Lau after he tested his recipes over a thousand times, was the first of its kind in the U.S., and the Mills 50 shop is where the jiggly obsession took hold. Each souffle pancake is made to order: egg whites whipped to soft peaks, cooked low and slow until it wobbles like a cloud. Tiramisu, creme brulee, matcha white chocolate, they all arrive theatrical and disappear fast. Save it for when happiness is the entire agenda.

places.name: Gideon's Bakehouse (Disney Springs Flagship)
places.address: Disney Springs
places.description: Steve Lewis started baking cookies in his kitchen and ended up with the hardest line in Disney Springs. These are nearly half-pound handmade monsters that take over 24 hours to prepare, and the Original Chocolate Chip alone converted a city of cynics. But Gideon's is bigger than the cookies: a candlelit, Edward Gorey Victorian bakehouse where a gargoyle guards the case and the cold brew is serious business. Go early, go hungry, and don't skip the cake slices.

faqs.q: Do you need reservations for Gideon's Bakehouse?
faqs.a: No reservations - it's a virtual queue. Expect ~2 hours on weekdays and up to ~5 on weekends. Go during Hot Cookie Hours (2-3 PM and 7-8 PM); there's a 7-cookie limit.

faqs.q: How do I skip the Gideon's line?
faqs.a: You can't skip it, but sister savory spot Six Ravens next door at The Landing usually has a much shorter wait.

places.name: Golden Hour Wine
places.address: Golden Hour Wine, 1560 Lake Baldwin Ln, Orlando, FL 32814-6661
places.description: Owner Heather named it well: in her words, golden hour is a great time to drink wine, particularly here in Florida. This woman-owned neighborhood shop and bar in Baldwin Park stocks roughly 700 bottles of responsibly farmed, small-production natural wine, with a proud lean toward women producers, grower Champagne, German Riesling, alpine and island wines. Something is always open for tasting, and the staff will match a bottle to your mood, not just your menu. Sip at a table in the cozy shop or take the sunset home with you.

places.name: Grocery Los Hermanos
places.address: 4130 Curry Ford Rd, Orlando, FL 32806
places.description: Part market, part taqueria, all heart. Grocery Los Hermanos on Curry Ford is the family-owned Mexican spot where you can buy your chiles and spices, watch the butcher case, and then sit down for carne asada and al pastor tacos on fresh handmade tortillas that put most dedicated taco shops to shame. The dining corner is bright and art-filled, the aguas frescas are ice-cold, and the verde enchiladas have a kick locals keep coming back for. Grocery first, restaurant by destiny, exactly the kind of place Orlando runs on.

places.name: H Mart Orlando Food Hall
places.address: 7501 W Colonial Dr, Orlando, FL 32818
places.description: Florida's first H Mart opened in 2025, and the food hall inside just keeps growing. The 2026 expansion nearly doubled the stalls, and now the walk between the produce aisles runs past Korean corn dogs at Oh K-Dog, tteokbokki at JAWS Topokki, Japanese fried cutlets at Chidon, Korean-Chinese noodles at Paik's, hot-stone bowls at Myung Ga, Korean fried chicken at bb.q, mala dishes at SORIMMARA, and hotteok filled pancakes at Seoul Hotteok. Shop for kimchi, gochujang and a whole wall of ramen, then eat your way through Seoul, Osaka and Beijing without leaving the building.

places.name: Harlow Grove
places.address: Winter Garden, FL 34787
places.description: Downtown Winter Garden's new social headquarters sits beneath a century-old oak, two stories of curated warmth where nobody checks the time. From the Knallhart Management Group, Harlow Grove runs on the philosophy of staying awhile: the downstairs bar hums with handcrafted cocktails like the Eden Spritz and HG Espresso Martini, the upstairs dining room serves comfort food with ambition, short rib dip, heirloom burrata, baby back ribs, lobster lasagna. The open-air terrace overlooks the town. Come for a weekday bite and accidentally stay through the night.

places.name: Hillstone Winter Park
places.address: Hillstone Restaurant, 215 S Orlando Ave, Winter Park, FL 32789-3657
places.description: Locals still call it Houston's, but whatever the sign says, this lakeside room on Lake Killarney is Winter Park's most dependable special-night table. Every seat faces the water, the sunsets do the decorating, and the family-run kitchen works a wood-burning grill on American classics done with real conviction: the Hawaiian ribeye that regulars plan weeks around, a French dip with a cult following, spinach and artichoke dip that arrives bubbling. The name comes from a Napa Valley vineyard. Time it for golden hour on the lake and you will understand the devotion.

places.name: House of Blues
places.address: Disney Springs
places.description: On Disney Springs' West Side, the House of Blues has been the city's rock club with a Southern accent since 1997. The Music Hall is general admission and standing room, which keeps you close enough to feel the drum hits, and the calendar runs the full spectrum, rock, hip hop, country, Latin, blues, tribute nights. Come early for Crossroads and eat shrimp and grits or jambalaya under the folk art of Mr. Imagination, then catch the gospel brunch on Sunday. There is Mississippi Delta mud under the stage, and some nights you can feel it.

places.name: Hunger Street Tacos
places.address: Hunger Street Tacos, 2103 W Fairbanks Ave, Winter Park, FL 32789-4507
places.description: Winter Park taco lovers treat this Fairbanks Avenue corner like a hometown pilgrimage site, and one bite explains why. Brothers Joe and David Creech built Hunger Street as a tribute to La Calle del Hambre in Mexico City, and their love letter is written in tender suadero on heirloom corn tortillas, tamal soaked in deep red mole, and the famous fried avocado taco that converts skeptics into regulars. Murals splash the walls inside and out, the outdoor seating keeps a convivial hum, and you can feel a family feeding you the recipes they grew up with.

places.name: ICON Park & The Orlando Eye
places.address: 8375 International Dr, Orlando, FL 32819
places.description: The whole I-Drive night skyline has a new compass point. ICON Park's 400-foot wheel lifts you above the city for a slow, twenty-minute soar with Orlando spread out in every direction, and the ground below keeps the energy going: SEA LIFE's ocean tunnel, Madame Tussauds, live music at Tin Roof, and SlingShot launching the brave 450 feet straight up. No gates, no ticket to wander in, just a park that keeps giving you reasons to stay.

places.name: Barbarella Orlando
places.address: 4141 John Young Pkwy Ste 3, Orlando, FL
places.description: If downtown Orlando has a clubhouse for people who still buy records and argue about setlists, this is it. Independent Bar is a gritty, multi-level live music den on Orange Avenue where the calendar spins through themed nights, tribute bands, karaoke, and all the flavors of loud guitar, and the crowd shows up the way they always have: sleeves up, all in. Multiple bars and dance floors keep the energy circulating, the sound system earns its keep, and the whole place runs on the kind of loyalty you cannot buy, only earn.

places.name: Jaleo
places.address: Jaleo, 1482 E Buena Vista Dr, Orlando, FL 32830-8518
places.description: Of all the big-league chef outposts that have landed in Orlando, this is the one worth a pilgrimage. José Andrés built his largest Jaleo at Disney Springs, and it delivers Spain with real conviction: jamón sliced so thin it glistens, tapas that taste like a Madrid night out, and wood-fired paellas layered with saffron and garlic aioli that make a group dinner feel like a celebration. Roaming rumba guitarists on Sundays, a sangria hour at the Matador Bar, and Pepe's bocatas next door for the grab-and-go version. This is the rare celebrity restaurant that eats like a love letter.

places.name: Jiang's Kitchen
places.address: 27 E Robinson St, Orlando, FL 32801
places.description: Watch your dinner get folded. Eric Jiang brought this downtown newcomer to the Arts District with one promise front and center: soup dumplings made by hand in an open kitchen, right where you can see every pleat pressed. That first bite, when the rich broth floods out over delicate pork, beef, shrimp, or crab, is the kind of moment that turns a casual weeknight into a memory. Around the dumplings sits a menu of authentic Shanghai cooking and sushi, plus a full bar, all from an owner whose family already runs some of the area's most respected Asian kitchens.

places.name: Juju
places.address: 700 Maguire Blvd, Orlando, FL
places.description: Do not let the converted Pizza Hut roofline fool you: inside this oddity is the most exciting Japanese room in Orlando. Juju shares the same playful spirit as its sibling Susuru but raises the game, an izakaya menu for the adventurous, and a tiny kappo counter where the chefs build original kaiseki-style courses. Dry-aged sashimi is the revelation, two-week-aged king salmon and otoro finished with Kaluga caviar tasting deeper than you thought fish could. The chawanmushi arrives crowned with lobster head dashi, pure theater. Booking the counter is the move, and you will talk about it for weeks.

places.name: Kabooki Sushi
places.address: Kabooki Sushi, 7705 Turkey Lake Rd, Orlando, FL 32819-5221
places.description: Ask any serious sushi lover in Orlando to name the room that leveled up the whole scene and this name comes up first. Chef Henry Moso leads Kabooki with a restless, globe-trotting approach: meticulous Japanese technique with creative freedom to borrow from everywhere, plated with genuine artistry. The traditional kaiseki multi-course option is the deep end, while the broader menu rewards adventurous ordering with combinations you will not see twice. The lounge out back keeps things sultry, and the whole place hums with the confidence of a restaurant that has stayed at the top by never repeating itself.

places.name: Kabooki Sushi Downtown
places.address: Downtown
places.description: The Kabooki name carries serious weight in Orlando, and the downtown location brings that reputation to the city center. Same philosophy: chef-driven sushi with meticulous technique and a creative streak that pulls from beyond Japan, served in a room built for a night out. The kaiseki multi-course experience remains the connoisseur's move, the rolls and crudos deliver spectacle and precision in equal measure, and the lounge energy means this is as much a downtown evening destination as it is a dinner. When the occasion matters, Orlando trusts Kabooki.

places.name: Kadence
places.address: 1809 Winter Park Rd, Orlando, FL 32803
places.description: A tiny counter, a Michelin star, and the room where Orlando's sushi dreams come true. What started in 2014 as a tiny sushi stand in Audubon Park has grown into one of Florida's most decorated dining rooms, where the owners' Michelin training and certified sake expertise shape a secret omakase that changes with the seasons. Each course lands in front of you, beautifully plated and built for the brave, fatty tuna, yuzu pepper scallops, whatever the chefs are obsessed with this week. Intimate, romantic, and worth every minute of the wait for a reservation.

places.name: Kaya
places.address: 618 N Thornton Ave, Orlando, FL 32803
places.description: This is the restaurant that made Orlando fall in love with Filipino food. Chef Lordfer Lalicon, a veteran of Michelin-starred kitchens including Blue Hill, teamed with Jamilyn Salonga Bailey to build something personal: casual fine dining in Mills 50 where Filipino techniques meet Florida's farms and waters. "Kaya natin" means we can, and the kitchen cooks like it believes it, seafood and vegetable-focused plates full of color, plus crowd-pleasers like ube pancakes and adobo fried rice that keep tables smiling. The room feels like a family dinner with really good taste.

places.name: Kelly Park / Rock Springs Run
places.address: Kelly Park Rd E & Rock Springs Rd, Apopka, FL 32712
places.description: A short drive out, Florida hands you its best natural water park for free. Rock Springs pours out of the earth at Kelly Park, a gushing channel so clear it looks lit from within, and the tubing run downstream is the laziest, loveliest half hour you can spend in Central Florida. Dr. Howard Kelly, a Johns Hopkins founder, gave this land to the people of Apopka in 1927, and it still feels like a gift. Paddle the Emerald Cut for jungle-walled seclusion, watch for turtles and otters, then hike. On a hot day, nothing else comes close.

faqs.q: What time should I arrive at Kelly Park / Rock Springs?
faqs.a: Line up by 5-6:30 AM on summer weekends - the park issues ~280 morning entry vouchers and regularly hits capacity before 9 AM. Entry is $3-5 per car; bring your own tube or rent on site.

places.name: Kia Center (formerly Amway Center)
places.address: 400 W Church St, Orlando, FL 32801
places.description: Orlando's beating heart sits at Church Street. The Kia Center, home of the Orlando Magic and the Solar Bears, is the arena that anchored downtown's revival, and Magic fans keep voting it one of the NBA's best game-night experiences in the league. Beyond basketball and hockey, the biggest touring acts in the world stop here, and the building itself is worth a look, with hundreds of works of art woven through its concourses. Whether you bleed Magic blue or just want the roar of a sold-out show, this is the room where the city gathers loudest.

places.name: King Bao
places.address: 710 N Mills Ave, Orlando, FL 32803
places.description: Mills 50 has its hole-in-the-wall hero and it serves steamed buns with attitude. King Bao claims Orlando's first quick-service gourmet bao title, and the proof is in a menu that plays by no one's rules: the pork-belly loaded Hogzilla, zesty Firecracker Shrimp, a Cuban bao that tastes like a Miami daydream, Nashville hot chicken with real fire, and crispy Fire tots for the table. Early-2000s metal rattles the speakers, the wall art keeps things trippy, and the self-serve kiosk keeps the line moving fast. Loud, cheap, and genuinely fun.

places.name: Knife & Spoon
places.address: Knife & Spoon, 4012 Central Florida Pkwy, Orlando, FL 32837-7662
places.description: This is the room that put Orlando fine dining on the Michelin map. Chef John Tesar, the two-time Top Chef contestant Bourdain called the most talented cook he ever worked with, built Knife & Spoon inside the Ritz-Carlton Grande Lakes around a simple idea: knife for beef, spoon for seafood. The dry-aged program is legendary, steaks aged for weeks or even months until the flavor turns nutty and profound, while the seafood side spans Florida catches and Japanese imports. The tuna and foie gras appetizer is famous for a reason. Elegant without being stiff, the meal that convinces skeptics.

places.name: Kres Chophouse
places.address: Kres Chophouse, 17 Church St W, Orlando, FL 32801-3301
places.description: Inside a 1930s Church Street landmark with original architecture to match, Kres has been downtown's power-steakhouse for years, and it wears the title with swagger. Their own line says it best: not your father's steakhouse. Prime beef is aged in-house and hand-cut to order, the Filet Wellington arrives flawless, and daily Florida coastal fish keeps the seafood side honest. There is even a full vegan menu, oysters Rockefeller included, which tells you how confident this kitchen is. Walkable from the Kia Center and Dr. Phillips, it is the classic pre-show or special-occasion move.

places.name: Kung Fu Kitchen
places.address: Kungfu Kitchen, 8466 Palm Pkwy, Orlando, FL 32836-6431
places.description: This is where the soup dumpling obsession starts. A Flushing, New York export, Kung Fu Kitchen built its Orlando following on two obsessions: noodles and bao, both made the hard way. Hand-pulled ramen and knife-cut noodles land springy and fresh in soup or stir-fried, and the xiao long bao arrive delicate and soup-filled, pork, chicken, or crab. Pan-fried Shanghai pork buns are the order that makes the table go quiet, and the chocolate xiao long bao tastes like cake batter in dumpling form. Red walls, cozy booths, and locations across town: a noodle run worth planning.

places.name: Lake Eola Park & Linton E. Allen Memorial Fountain
places.address: Lake Eola Park, 512 E Washington St, Orlando, FL 32801-1941
places.description: This is the lake Orlando sees in its dreams. The swans glide past the paddle boats, the fountain throws light and water into the downtown skyline, and the 0.9 mile loop around the shore might be the most walked path in the city. Come for a slow stroll, stay for a concert under the stars in the Walt Disney Amphitheater, and linger for the Sunday farmers market. Few places gather a whole city the way this park does.

faqs.q: How much are the swan boats at Lake Eola, and when are they open?
faqs.a: Swan pedal boats run about $15 for 30 minutes, Tuesday-Sunday 10 AM-7 PM (closed Mondays), no reservations - first come, first served. A rainbow boat joined the fleet in June 2026.

places.name: Level 99
places.address: Disney Springs
places.description: Forget everything you thought you knew about the old NBA Experience building: it is now the largest interactive gaming playground of its kind in the country. Level99 packs a warehouse of life-sized mini-games, from axe-dodging beams to logic puzzles to head-to-head duels, all unlocked by an RFID wristband at check-in. Team up for cooperative challenge rooms, settle scores in player-vs-player duels, or hunt through the art scavenger hunt. The bar keeps craft cocktails and local beers flowing, and the scratch kitchen's Detroit-style pizza is dangerously good fuel between rounds. Pure group fun.

places.name: Lipa Rooftop
places.address: Lipa Rooftop, 3001 Sherberth Rd, Kissimmee, FL 34747-1787
places.description: Celebrity chef Akira Back built his Orlando flag atop the ette hotel in Celebration, and the view does half the talking: on a clear night you can watch the Disney fireworks bloom over the skyline from your table. The menu is Asian haute cuisine with Back's signature polish, sushi and specialty rolls like the Dream Girl, citrus-spiced shrimp, and mochi to finish, paired with craft cocktails and a DJ keeping the energy high. Stunning decor, a real sense of occasion, and the only rooftop in Kissimmee playing at this level. Book a Friday or Saturday and dress the part.

places.name: Little Sister Dumpling
places.address: Mills 50, Orlando, FL
places.description: Mills 50 does dumplings the way only Mills 50 can: small, confident, and serious about craft. Little Sister Dumpling is the district's new dumpling specialist on North Mills Avenue, an Asian fusion kitchen working through Korean-inflected flavors alongside classic techniques. Everything is hand-folded and made to be eaten immediately, which is the whole point of a dumpling done right. Slide into a seat along Mills, order a spread to share, and taste why the district keeps turning out spots like this. A welcome addition to Orlando's best foodie street.

places.name: Lukes Kitchen and Bar
places.address: Luke's Kitchen and Bar, 640 Orlando Ave S, Maitland, FL 32751-5612
places.description: Maitland's favorite everyday celebration. From the team behind Winter Park's beloved Luma on Park and Prato, Luke's is chef Brandon McGlamery's love letter to classic American cooking with a chef's playful brain. The blackened fish collar and Cheshire pork chop over goat-cheese boursin grits are the signatures, PB&J spare ribs and a towering shellfish starter keep the adventurous happy, and locals insist this is the best patio in Maitland. Neighborhood prices, craft cocktails with house-made ingredients, and a room that feels like the dinner party you always want to be invited to. It earns its regulars.

places.name: Lumenes Catering
places.address: West Orlando
places.description: Look for the light blue truck on West Colonial: it is carrying some of the best Haitian food in Orlando. Lumene's runs as a food truck and catering company, and the menu is the real deal, griot with crispy edges and tender insides, falling-off-the-bone oxtail, fried whole snapper, and the earthy black rice (diri djondjon) that keeps regulars coming back. Haitian mac, sweet plantains, a hit of pikliz, and fresh pineapple juice round it out. Fans call it the best Haitian food in town, and the portions are generous enough to feed you twice.

places.name: Luminescent
places.address: Luminescent, 12286 E Colonial Dr, Orlando, FL 32826-4709
places.description: East Orlando's day-to-night dream. Luminescent runs a dual life that actually works: a polished, Indian-influenced coffee bar by day, a craft cocktail lounge after dark, all wrapped around a deep-green bar in a room people call impeccable. The drinks are where it gets special, a Keral's Kulfi built on pistachio cold foam and soan papdi, traditional chā, affogatos with real kulfi ice cream, plus pistachio, cardamom, and rose water weaving through both the espresso and the cocktails. Come in the morning to work, come back at night to unwind. A rare two-visit place.

places.name: Magic Kingdom Park
places.address: Disney's Magic Kingdom, 1180 Seven Seas Dr, Orlando, FL 32830
places.description: You know this park before you ever set foot in it, and it still gets you. Cinderella Castle at the hub of six lands, Space Mountain's rattling darkness, the Haunted Mansion's stretching rooms, pirates singing their pirate song: these are not rides so much as shared memories the whole country grew up with. Locals come back for the fireworks, the Festival of Fantasy parade, and the electric joy of watching a child's first visit through your own eyes. However many times you have been, Main Street still does something to you. Plan for a full day and give in.

places.name: Mango's Tropical Cafe
places.address: Mango's Tropical Cafe, 8126 International Dr, Orlando, FL 32819-9323
places.description: Ask anyone who came for dinner and stayed till close. Mango's Tropical Cafe took everything it learned on South Beach's Ocean Drive and rebuilt it bigger on International Drive, and the legend grew with the room. Supper-club dining under a waterfall of live Latin music, dancers, and handcrafted cocktails, then the whole building becomes the nightclub. It's the only spot on I-Drive where dinner, a show, and a dance floor were never separate plans.

places.name: Mecatos
places.address: Winter Park, FL 32789
places.description: Colombia, flown in fresh. Mecatos is Orlando's Colombian gathering place, a bakery and cafe that flies its coffee beans straight from Colombia so your cup tastes like the highlands. The Winter Park location on Morse Boulevard pairs that coffee with warm, cheese-pull pan de bono, crispy empanadas, guava-and-cheese pastries, and a strawberry napoleon regulars rave about. The covered patio makes lingering easy, and the kitchen runs breakfast through dinner with traditional dishes and sandwiches. Coffee harvested, roasted, and rushed to your table with real Colombian pride. Orlando's Colombian community has made it theirs; you should too.

places.name: Mengs Kitchen
places.address: Meng's Kitchen, 2415 E Colonial Dr, Orlando, FL 32803-5018
places.description: The best seat in the house is inside a grocery store. Meng's Kitchen hides in the back of iFresh Market on East Colonial, a tiny stall cooking some of Orlando's most soulful Southeast Asian food. The Hainan chicken and rice combo, poached and fried, is the move; the five-spice roasted chicken and golden crispy pork belly have real devotees, and the katsu curry and panang oxtail keep things bold. Seating is tiny, so take it to go and eat like royalty at home. The Infatuation put it on the map for a reason: this is street-food flavor with home-kitchen heart.

places.name: Mohawk Smokehouse
places.address: Central Florida
places.description: The best barbecue in Orlando might come from a guy who learned to cook beside his Italian grandma. Tyler Evans and his wife Sarah launched Mohawk Smokehouse in 2022 with a mission they call craft BBQ with southern roots, and critics have taken notice, including a Critic's Choice nod for Orlando's best BBQ. Central Texas-style beef brisket with serious bark and marble sits alongside Southern comfort like shrimp and grits, everything built from fresh, locally sourced ingredients. They run pop-ups, events, and a growing catering business, and the brisket alone is worth chasing down their schedule.

places.name: Morimoto Asia
places.address: Morimoto Asia, 1600 E Buena Vista Dr, Orlando, FL 32830
places.description: Iron Chef in the flesh, and the grand opening set the tone: Morimoto himself cracked a sacred sake cask and turned a 100-pound tuna into a 60-foot maki roll. A decade later, Morimoto Asia remains one of Disney Springs' most striking rooms, a two-story dining hall where the chef's first pan-Asian menu plays out in dim sum, pristine sushi, and a bar program built around sake, including the famous sake sangria. The kitchen and prep space famously run bigger than the dining room, which tells you where the priorities are. Polished, theatrical, and genuinely delicious.

places.name: Mosonori
places.address: Mosonori, 7541 W Sand Lake Rd, Orlando, FL 32819-5109
places.description: Chef Henry Moso, the genius behind Kabooki, did something radical for the I-Drive corridor: he opened a handroll bar. Mosonori on Sand Lake is all about temaki, one handroll at a time, served directly from the chef's hands to yours so the nori stays shatteringly crisp. The Moso Omakase set runs you through hamachi, lobster, akami, toro, and eel, and the tastings, toro tartare, hamachi with ponzu and yuzu oil, show off aged fish at its best. Calm, minimalist, and quietly thrilling. Sit at the bar, order the set, thank us later.

places.name: Museum of Ice Cream
places.address: 9101 International Dr, Orlando, FL 32819
places.description: The pinkest thing to ever hit International Drive. The world-famous Museum of Ice Cream is planting its flag at Pointe Orlando, and the concept is pure joy: a multi-sensory playground where unlimited ice cream meets Instagram bait, from the iconic sprinkle pool to ice-cream history exhibits, carnival games, a giant slide, and even a diner pouring cocktails for the grown-ups. Since its 2016 New York pop-up days it has been a sugar rush of interactive rooms, and Orlando, the family-fun capital, is its natural home. Check opening status before you roll up with the kids: it is worth the trip.

places.name: Nami
places.address: Nami, 6004 Artist Ave, Orlando, FL 32827
places.description: Lake Nona's Wave Hotel hides one of Orlando's most transporting dining rooms. Nami, a Michelin-recommended contemporary Japanese restaurant, is built around drama done right: a backlit, undulating wooden ceiling, Japanese maple trees anchoring the room, and a sleek bar made for lingering. The menu goes bold and global, lobster donuts, BBQ eel donburi, A5 steak, refined small plates that keep surprising, and the separate Chef's Counter turns dinner into an extended chef-led tasting. Precision, artistry, and a cocktail program with tableside flair. Dress up and make it a night.

places.name: New General
places.address: New General, 155 E New England Ave, Winter Park, FL 32789-4330
places.description: Part café, part modern general store, entirely Winter Park charm. New General on New England Avenue is the health-forward hangout where clean ingredients meet genuinely great coffee: the blueberry lavender latte is the drink everyone tells their friends about, the matcha and cold brew are dialed in, and the Blue Majik latte brings a little theater to your cup. Shroom avo toast, acai bowls, frittatas, and gluten-friendly everything keep the food side fresh, and while you wait you can browse shelves of small-batch soaps, granolas, and goods. Plant-filled, bright, and quietly the feel-good room of the neighborhood.

places.name: Nile Ethiopian
places.address: Nile Ethiopian, 7048 International Dr, Orlando, FL 32819-8222
places.description: International Drive's best-kept dinner secret. Family-run Nile has been serving traditional Ethiopian cuisine since 2006, and it remains the kind of place regulars describe as the best meal they have had in Orlando. Everything is shared, mounded on spongy injera that you tear and scoop, from the vegan Taste of the Nile with its shiro, lentils, and collard greens to the Chef's Special with doro wat, kitfo, and sizzling beef tibs. The room is warm and lovely, and if you can catch the traditional coffee ceremony, do not skip it. A genuinely cultural evening hiding in plain sight on I-Drive.

places.name: Noir Bar
places.address: 861 N Orange Ave, Orlando, FL 32801 (inside Talay Thai)
places.description: To find Noir, first you find the Thai restaurant. Tucked behind a hidden door inside Talay Thai downtown, this is Orlando's true speakeasy moment: dark, moody, and made for date night. The craft cocktails are the star, creative blends like a pandan and matcha number that tastes as intriguing as it sounds, and the Thai-inspired bites keep pace. Dim lighting, lush decor, and the quiet thrill of a place most walkers-by will never know exists. Dine at Talay first, then slip through the wall and let the evening shift into something cinematic.

places.name: Nomikai by Sushi Saint
places.address: ICON Park, 8375 International Dr
places.description: Chef Michael Collantes, behind Michelin-starred Soseki and Bib Gourmand Sushi Saint, just went big. Nomikai by Sushi Saint at ICON Park is his boldest concept yet, and the name says it all: the Japanese art of the celebratory gathering, food and drink and friends. Sushi Saint's greatest hits show up, salmon aguachile, hamachi truffle potato, a large-format omakase platter, joined by shareable showstoppers like dry-aged tomahawk and lobster noodles. The room is his "Tokyo neo-cyberpunk" vision, neon blues, original art, dark and moody with electronica. Local chefs planting a flag on I-Drive: this is how the tourist corridor grows up.

places.name: Norigami
places.address: Norigami, 426 W Plant St, Winter Garden, FL 34787-3014
places.description: A tiny counter and a streak of Michelin Bib Gourmands: Winter Garden's Norigami proves great things come in the smallest rooms. Chef David Tsan works with surgical precision inside Plant Street Market, where the name, nori plus origami, becomes a ritual: every piece of sushi arrives on colorful washi paper that guests fold into cranes for the growing centerpiece bowl. The omakase is the move, popcorn hamachi and toro carpaccio with truffle among the standouts, the rice seasoned and loosely packed just right. Polished, warm, and worth the trip west. Book ahead, the counter fills fast.

places.name: Oga's Cantina
places.address: Disney's Hollywood Studios
places.description: This is not your ordinary cantina: Oga's sits inside Galaxy's Edge at Hollywood Studios, and it is the bar every Star Wars fan dreams about. Droid DJ R-3X spins from behind the bar, the cocktails arrive in otherworldly presentations, and the famous Fuzzy Tauntaun literally makes your mouth tingle. Bespin Fizz, Outer Rim, and non-alcoholic concoctions for the younglings, plus galactic snacks to keep you grounded. Space is tight and the vibe is electric, part Mos Eisley, part house party, and the hardest reservation at Hollywood Studios. Book ahead and channel your inner smuggler.

places.name: Orlando International Airport (MCO)
places.address: 1 Jeff Fuqua Blvd, Orlando, FL 32827
places.description: The trip starts or ends here, and lately it is eating well. Orlando International has quietly built one of the better airport food scenes in the country, and it keeps getting more local: 4Rivers smokehouse barbecue, Black Bean Deli's Cuban sandwiches, Otto's High Dive cocktails, Maxine's on Shine from Thornton Park, Kelly's Homemade Ice Cream, Seito Sushi, and Smoke & Donuts bringing brisket and crullers together like nobody else. The iconic carpet is still the first photo, but your last taste of Orlando can now be genuinely delicious. Build in a buffer and eat here, not on the plane.

places.name: Orlando Science Center & The Dome
places.address: 777 E Princeton St, Orlando, FL 32803
places.description: Every Orlando kid of the last thirty years has a Science Center memory, and they all involve that dome. The Orlando Science Center started in 1960 as the Central Florida Museum and grew into four floors of hands-on wonder in Loch Haven Park: dinosaur digs, a living cypress swamp, the observatory roof. But The Dome by Dr. Phillips Charities is the place's soul, a 300-seat giant dome theater that swallows you whole in Everest climbs and ocean depths with images bigger than your peripheral vision. Go learn something and feel like a kid again.

places.name: The Osprey
places.address: The Osprey, 4899 New Broad St, Orlando, FL 32814-6629
places.description: Baldwin Park's most beloved dining room. The Osprey, the Good Salt Group's New Broad Street anchor since 2015, is that rare room that does everything well: an open kitchen, a buzzing central bar, and New American cooking with a seafood soul. Comfort classics like cottage pie and homemade bolognese share the menu with Florida fish, grilled oysters, and a thoughtful oyster-bar streak. The weekday happy hour with dollar oysters is local legend, desserts close things sweetly, and the chef's table experience rewards the truly committed. Impeccable service, lively but comfortable, and a decade of loyalty to prove it.

places.name: Osteria Ester
places.address: 629 E Central Blvd, Orlando, FL
places.description: The Good Salt crew keeps landing in the right rooms. Osteria Ester, from the team behind the Osprey and Seito Sushi, takes over the old Soco space on East Central and turns it into a love letter to chef-partner Michael Cooper's grandmother: classic Italian-American cooking in a warm, neighborhood setting. Fresh pasta, house-baked focaccia, and the kind of unpretentious hospitality that made the group's other rooms famous. This is the Italian joint you can live with: date nights, family tables, and that perfect post-work glass. Worth a look in Thornton Park to see what this team does next.

places.name: Otto's High Dive
places.address: 2304 E Robinson St, Orlando, FL 32803
places.description: A rum bar with a soul. Otto's High Dive, named for co-owner Giovanni Fernandez's grandfather, who poured drinks in Manzanillo, Cuba during the cocktail golden age, channels that heritage into a Milk District Cuban rum bar with Bib Gourmand recognition. Ropa vieja and lechon asado sit next to Florida seafood and a serious raw bar, and the rum program is the point: classic daiquiris, inventive house builds, and a list that takes the 1950s Havana canon seriously. Café Abundancia covers the mornings, daily brunch the weekends, and the dim, greenery-lined room hums with date-night energy. Book ahead; walk-ins wait.

places.name: Palm Beach Meats
places.address: Palm Beach Meats, 3421 Orange Ave S, Orlando, FL 32806-6127
places.description: Florida's only all-Wagyu shop and restaurant, now on South Orange. Eric and Meghan San Pedro's Palm Beach Meats is built on one obsession: Japanese, Australian, and American Wagyu, done every way. The counter serves a Wagyu burger that eats like a revelation and a layered Frito Pie, Filipino-leaning comfort like Wagyu tapa over garlic rice with a fried egg, a Wagyu Philly, and a beef-tallow Nutella brownie people go back for. Out front it is fast casual; behind the coolers is a full market with Wagyu deli cuts and frozen beef. For carnivores, this is a pilgrimage spot.

places.name: Park Avenue Historic District
places.address: Park Ave, Winter Park, FL 32789
places.description: This is the postcard Orlando never sends, a brick-lined avenue under a canopy of old oaks where the shopfronts have stood since the twenties. Winter Park's Park Avenue made the National Register of Historic Places for good reason: every block feels like a small southern city that refused to be paved over. Stroll it slowly, peek down the side alleys, let a boutique you never planned to enter steal an hour. Locals measure everything else in Orlando against this street, and everything else falls a little short.

places.name: Peach Valley Cafe
places.address: Peach Valley Cafe, 2849 S Orange Ave, Orlando, FL 32806-5403
places.description: The apple fritters arrive hot enough to burn your fingers, and you will not care. Peach Valley has been Central Florida's neighborhood brunch answer since 2001, the rare local chain that still cooks like someone's name is on the sign. Chicken and waffles with blueberry butter and a Cajun-spiked syrup, shrimp and grits that taste of the low country, and a sunlit porch made for slow mornings. Bring the whole crew. Everyone finds a plate that feels like it was made just for them.

places.name: Perla's Pizza, Vinyl Records & Cocktail Bar
places.address: 959 W Fairbanks Ave, Winter Park, FL 32789
places.description: A thin, crackling crust that shatters like a good secret, playlists spun live on vinyl, and a cocktail in your hand while the pies fly. Perla's is the Florida Man of pizza joints in the best way: chef-driven, joyfully nontraditional, and curated by Michelin-starred chef Mike Collantes. There is a banana-topped pie on the menu and somehow it works. There is a tikka-spiced pie and somehow it works better. Come for the slice, stay because the room has the easy, spinning-record buzz of a party that never tips over.

places.name: Permanent Vacation
places.address: Permanent Vacation, 106 Lake Ave, Maitland, FL 32751-6424
places.description: Walk into the Copper Rocket, find the door marked Employees Only, push it open, and Florida disappears. Permanent Vacation is a tiki speakeasy hidden inside a Maitland sports bar, and it commits completely: skulls and bamboo, fish floats in netting overhead, fog that rolls through the dark while your bartender, billed as a travel agent, hands you a rum cocktail and your tab in a passport. The Pearl Necklace is the one people talk about. Reserve ahead. The people who find this place tend to come back like they are checking in on an old flame.

places.name: Pho Hoa
places.address: Pho Hoa, 649 N Primrose Dr, Orlando, FL 32803-5016
places.description: On a side street off Colonial, this is where Orlando goes when it wants Vietnamese food without the performance. Pho Hoa is a bright, family-style room built around a broth that tastes like someone refused to cut a single corner: deep, clear, alive with star anise. The pho bo is the order you will see at half the tables, the bun bo hue brings a slow chili warmth, and the Vietnamese iced coffee is thick enough to stand a spoon in. Unfussy, generous, and exactly the kind of place locals quietly depend on.

places.name: Pizza Bruno
places.address: Pizza Bruno, 3990 Curry Ford Rd, Orlando, FL 32806-2702
places.description: Order the garlic knots first and thank everyone later. Pizza Bruno is owner Bruno Zacchini's love letter to the Jersey shore summers that taught him dough, turned into a wood-fired Neapolitan room on Curry Ford Road. The crust is naturally leavened, blistered and chewy, and the whole place hums with neighborhood conviction, the kind of pizzeria where the staff genuinely cares whether your slice lands. The pies are playful but never gimmicky: tight technique, honest Italian soul, and a second location in College Park for when the craving hits west of the tracks.

places.name: Pomelo
places.address: 1632 N Mills Ave, Orlando, FL 32803
places.description: This is the one every Orlando food person has been watching. Top Chef season three winner Hung Huynh, the Saigon-born chef who cooked at Per Se and Guy Savoy, is building his first full-scale Orlando restaurant in Mills 50: a live-fire Southeast Asian room called Pomelo. Expect grilled seafood, skewers, and charred octopus, plus a cocktail program built around the pomelo fruit, lemongrass, and regional herbs. In his words it will be chill, fun, and loud, and if the durian shows up, funky. Watch @pomelo.fl for the opening date. This one will be a scene.

places.name: Prato
places.address: Prato, 124 N Park Ave, Winter Park, FL 32789
places.description: Right on Park Avenue, with window-paned doors thrown open to the brick street, Prato is Winter Park's idea of Italian and it is a good one. House-made pastas, wood-fired pies, and a long bar that practically begs you to linger. The mustard spaghettini cacio e pepe is the dish people drive across town for, peppery and silky in equal measure, and the pretzel-crusted calamari proves a pub snack can be elegant. A Michelin-selected room that never feels stiff, only sunlit, generous, and alive.

places.name: Raglan Road
places.address: Disney Springs
places.description: The room itself was built in Ireland and shipped to Orlando, mahogany and walnut salvaged from old Irish bars and churches, and you can feel it. Raglan Road is Disney Springs' answer to a real Dublin pub, named for the Kavanagh poem that U2 and Van Morrison turned into song. There are live bands and Irish dancers nightly, a rollicking weekend brunch show, fish and chips that people genuinely cross the property for, and a whiskey list that takes its job seriously. It is the rare Disney Springs room that locals bring out-of-towners to and stay for themselves.

places.name: Ramen Takagi
places.address: Ramen Takagi, 3635 Aloma Ave, Oviedo, FL 32765-6395
places.description: Out in Oviedo, far from the ramen crowds, sits a small shop that serious noodle people will drive across the county for. Ramen Takagi cooks everything from scratch in a space that feels like someone's kitchen that happens to serve the public. The black garlic tonkotsu is the signature, deep and savory with that roasted edge, the spicy miso brings real heat, and the tantan mazesoba proves they can do brothless too. Everything arrives made from the heart. Go at lunch, order warm, and plan to return for the whole menu.

places.name: Ravello
places.address: Four Seasons Resort Orlando
places.description: This is the kind of Italian dinner you plan a birthday around. Ravello sits inside the Four Seasons Resort Orlando, where executive chef Fabrizio Schenardi, a Torino native, runs a kitchen that makes its pastas, breads, sauces, and desserts entirely in house. The veal ravioli is the signature, soft and rich the way holiday meals are remembered, and the wood-fired pies come layered with prosciutto di Parma and fresh burrata. It even holds a rare Italian taste certification few American restaurants ever earn. Bring someone you want to impress. The room will help.

places.name: Reyes Mezcaleria
places.address: Reyes Mezcaleria, 821 N Orange Ave, Orlando, FL 32801-1014
places.description: Chef Wendy Lopez, a Michoacán native, cooks the Mexico she grew up with and pours it alongside more than 150 agave spirits, and the whole room hums with that kind of intention. The Good Salt Restaurant Group, the family behind some of Orlando's most loved dining rooms, founded Reyes in 2017 with one mission: honor the cuisine, the spirits, and the culture of Mexico. Every plate feels rooted, every pour feels considered. This is Mexican cooking with soul and a bar with real depth.

places.name: Rion's Ocean Room
places.address: Rion's Ocean Room, 3201 Corrine Dr, Winter Park, FL 32803-2224
places.description: Tucked inside East End Market, Rion's Ocean Room is a walk-up poke counter that does one thing and does it honestly. The fish is cut fresh and treated with respect: premium ahi, fatty salmon, ono, Hawaiian tobiko style, and the curious inari bombs that regulars talk about like folklore. Order it over perfectly cooked rice or buy it by the pound like you mean it. No frills, just glistening fish and clean flavor. This is Orlando's quiet proof that you do not need an ocean to eat like you have one.

places.name: Salt & Cellar
places.address: Salt & the Cellar by Akira Back, 3001 Sherberth Rd, Kissimmee, FL 34747-1787
places.description: Inside the Ette Hotel in Kissimmee, chef Akira Back has built one of those dim, polished rooms that makes an evening feel like an occasion before the first course lands. Salt & the Cellar moves across steakhouse, Mediterranean, and Japanese-leaning Asian flavors with the confidence of a chef who has cooked on big stages. Table lamps, smart service, and a Sunday afternoon tea that guests talk about long after. If you want a date-night room that actually delivers on the promise of its lighting, this is the one south of Disney.

places.name: Seby's Pizza
places.address: Seby's Pizza, 1555 Semoran Blvd, Winter Park, FL 32792-1501
places.description: Chef Sebastian "Seby" Donofrio is a third-generation Italian-American making the New York pie he grew up on, in a tiny plaza where Casselberry fades into Winter Park. The menu reads like a love letter to Manhattan street names: the Soho, the Rubirosa, the Nolita, each one a thin, foldable, hand-tossed slice with house-made dough and a scratch sauce that stays honest, never sweet. He uses reverse-osmosis water and never-frozen mozzarella because he cares that much. Opened in 2025 and already spoken of like a neighborhood institution. The amaretto cream cake is the sleeper hit.

places.name: Seito Sushi
places.address: Seito Sushi, 8031 Turkey Lake Rd, Orlando, FL 32819-7382
places.description: On New Broad Street in Baldwin Park, Seito has spent more than two decades proving that sushi in Central Florida can be both traditional and fearlessly modern. Executive chef Huy Tin runs a kitchen that honors classic technique while inventing with it: tuna crispy rice with smoked trout roe, torch salmon, bluefin chutoro sashimi, and a six-course chef's tasting for the truly committed. The room is dim and elegant, the kind of place anniversaries default to. It is sushi as a quiet art form, and it has the staying power to prove it.

places.name: Selam Ethiopian
places.address: Selam, 5494 Central Florida Pkwy, Orlando, FL 32821-8774
places.description: Eating at Selam is a hands-on, tear-the-injera, scoop-with-your-fingers ceremony, and the room on Central Florida Parkway treats first-timers like honored guests. This Ethiopian and Eritrean kitchen serves the great wats and tibs on platters built for sharing, with a traditional buna coffee ritual that arrives at your table still fragrant from the roast. The staff will walk you through it all with genuine warmth, and the tej, a honey wine, is the right companion. Go with people you like, order the combination platter, and surrender to the communal joy of the table.

places.name: Selva Rosa
places.address: 901 S Orlando Ave, Winter Park, FL 32789
places.description: A jungle-gorgeous room in Maitland where two of the world's best food cultures collide and somehow land. Selva Rosa fuses Mexican and Japanese cooking with genuine imagination: birria tempura sushi, hamachi in bright green sauces, short rib taquizas, and a matcha mojito that people photograph before they taste. Tuesday brings the famous all-you-can-eat tacos and sushi night that has Maitland buzzing. It is the rare fusion spot that feels like a party you were lucky to get invited to, loud, colorful, and full of plates that make you stop talking.

places.name: Shin Jung
places.address: Mills 50
places.description: One of the first Korean restaurants in Orlando, serving the city since 1993, and still the benchmark. Shin Jung survived a fire and came back rebuilt, brighter, and better, and the room on Colonial hums with the sizzle of tabletop grills and K-pop on the screens. The banchan spread is generous, the LA kalbi and beef bulgogi carry real flame character, and the soon tofu stew arrives bubbling like it has something to prove. Michelin has taken notice. Go with a group, order for the table, and let dinner become an event.

places.name: Shiraz Market
places.address: Shiraz Market, 185 S Ronald Reagan Blvd, Longwood, FL 32750-5209
places.description: Half Persian grocery, half sizzling grill counter, all heart. Shiraz Market in Longwood is the kind of place where you come for spices and leave with a kebab platter you did not plan on. The hot food case holds tender chicken koobideh, beef kebabs, and falafel with all the mezze players, hummus, baba ganoush, all made with halal ingredients. Browse the shelves for Persian sweets and teas while your food hits the grill, then eat at the counter like a regular. Worth the detour up 17-92 every time.

places.name: Six Ravens
places.address: The Landing, Disney Springs
places.description: The people behind Gideon's Bakehouse finally went savory, and Disney Springs got better for it. Six Ravens, in The Landing, serves Coffyns, old-school hand pies made from house-baked yeast rolls and stuffed with chef-driven fillings. The menu reads like a love letter to Orlando's food scene: a Pizza Bruno collab with basil pesto chicken, a Smoke & Donuts mashup of pulled pork and mac and cheese, a Pink Salamander cheeseburger pie. Local draft beer from Sideward Brewing and The Ravenous Pig rounds it out. Dark, storybook, and built for grabbing and going between adventures.

places.name: Smoke & Donuts BBQ
places.address: 601 N Primrose Dr, Orlando, FL 32803
places.description: Chef Ian Russell is a Culinary Institute of America graduate who fell for roadside smoke on a cross-country trip, and his Milk District joint tastes like the trip was worth it. Smoke & Donuts pairs low-and-slow USDA Prime brisket, Carolina pulled pork, and brown butter turkey with made-to-order cake donuts, a pairing nobody else in town would dare. The Lou Donut is the legend: bourbon maple glaze, chocolate, and a topper of brisket burnt ends. Family-run since its pop-up days, casual, loud with classic rock, and deeply committed to feeding its neighborhood well.

places.name: Smokemade Meats + Eats
places.address: 1400 S Crystal Lake Dr, Orlando, FL 32806
places.description: Pitmaster Tyler Brunache learned Central Texas barbecue the hard way, running pop-ups in DC that sold out in minutes, then came home to Orlando and did it right. Smokemade, on Curry Ford West, is the real deal in the Texas tradition: concrete floors, a menu scrawled on butcher paper, and brisket that makes a Michelin Bib Gourmand look inevitable. Pork ribs in salt and pepper with a proper smoky edge, jalapeno-cheddar sausage that would hold its own in Lockhart, and house-baked bread alongside everything. Come hungry, thank the pitmaster, and plan your return before you finish eating.

places.name: Society Park
places.address: International Dr, Orlando, FL 32819
places.description: International Drive's newest social engine, dubbed the Gen Z country club, trades the golf course for something louder. Society Park is a sports and entertainment complex built around padel and pickleball: nine padel courts, an exhibition court, children's courts, and three pickleball courts, plus a pro shop, a spa, and two restaurants. The pitch is that your workout and your night out live in the same place now. Come for a match, stay for dinner, and enjoy a side of Orlando where being active and being social are the same thing.

places.name: Sodough Square
places.address: Sodough Square, 419 E Michigan St, Orlando, FL 32806-4511
places.description: A Detroit native built Orlando's best square slice, fittingly, on Michigan Street. SoDough Square serves authentic Detroit-style pizza with the caramelized cheese edge crackling down the corners of every pan, exactly the way owner Robert Bair remembers it from the Motor City. The menu leans playful: the Detroit Rob City with hot honey, a taco pizza, a Big Mac tribute, all with dough so good they sell out some days. There is now a Winter Park location too. Order early, thank the blue-collar pan, and do not skip the cheesy garlic bread.

places.name: Sorekara
places.address: Sorekara, 4979 New Broad St, Orlando, FL 32814-6414
places.description: Orlando's first two-Michelin-star restaurant hides on a Baldwin Park street, and dining there is closer to theater than dinner. Chef William Shen built Sorekara around Japan's 72 micro seasons, so the 20-plus course tasting menu reinvents itself every week or so, moving guests through multiple rooms over several hours. There is deep refinement here: Hokkaido crab, madai with a sly twist, desserts that close the night like a finale. And there is mischief too, a course that plays with a convenience-store snack run. One seating a night, a few nights a week, and worth every bit of planning it takes.

places.name: Soseki Modern Omakase
places.address: 955 W Fairbanks Ave, Winter Park, FL 32789
places.description: Ten seats, one chef's counter, and a Michelin star earned within a year of opening. Soseki is chef Michael Collantes' intimate omakase room on Fairbanks Avenue, where the finest fish from Japan meets the bounty of Central Florida on plates made by Florida artisans. Every piece of nigiri lands with precision and a story, and the tea pairing has its own following among those who skip the sake. This is dinner as a private performance, personal, playful, and precise. Book the moment you know you are going. Seats this small never wait around.

faqs.a: Book at sosekifl.com - tickets are nonrefundable, about $259 per person. Reserve far ahead; the 10-seat counter sells out.

places.name: Sparrow Orlando
places.address: Mills 50
places.description: A dark, moody little room in the North Quarter that feels like a library you can drink in.
